questions.q: A 35-year-old farmer presents with a painless ulcer with rolled edges on the dorsum of the hand, with regional lymphadenopathy. Gram stain shows a 'bamboo cane' appearance of the organism. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Cutaneous anthrax caused by Bacillus anthracis presents as a painless eschar with surrounding edema. The characteristic Gram stain appearance is 'bamboo cane' – large Gram-positive bacilli arranged end-to-end in chains.

questions.q: A 28-year-old immunocompromised patient develops a vesiculopustular eruption following the dermatomal distribution of T5. After healing, the patient complains of persistent burning pain. What mediator is primarily responsible for the pain?
questions.exp: Post-herpetic neuralgia (PHN) following Herpes Zoster is primarily mediated by Substance P, a neuropeptide involved in pain transmission. VZV damages sensory neurons, leading to central sensitization where Substance P plays a key role.

questions.q: A 22-year-old male presents with a genital ulcer that is soft, painful, and has a 'ragged' edge with a gray slough. The ulcer is associated with painful inguinal lymphadenopathy. What is the causative organism?
questions.exp: Chancroid is caused by Haemophilus ducreyi. It presents with a soft, painful, ragged ulcer with an undermined edge and gray slough, often accompanied by painful inguinal lymphadenopathy (bubo). The ulcer of syphilis is painless.

questions.q: A 40-year-old male from rural India presents with hypopigmented patches with loss of sensation over the cheek. Slit skin smear shows 1–10 organisms per high-power field (BI of 2). Which category does this fall under as per Ridley-Jopling classification?
questions.exp: Borderline tuberculoid (BT) leprosy has a bacteriological index (BI) of 1–2+ on slit skin smear. BT patches are more numerous, less well-defined, and satellite lesions may be present, unlike the single, well-defined patch of TT leprosy.

questions.q: A 55-year-old woman presents with recurrent oral ulcers, skin erosions over the trunk, and positive Nikolsky's sign. Direct immunofluorescence shows intercellular IgG deposits in a 'chicken-wire' pattern. Which antigen is targeted?
questions.exp: Pemphigus vulgaris targets Desmoglein 3 (mucocutaneous type). The 'chicken-wire' or 'fishnet' pattern on DIF with intercellular IgG deposits is characteristic. Mucosal involvement primarily involves Dsg3, while skin involvement includes both Dsg1 and Dsg3.

questions.q: A patient presents with tense bullae on erythematous skin in the axilla and groin. DIF shows linear IgG and C3 at the basement membrane zone. The antibody is directed against the NC16A domain. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Bullous pemphigoid (BP) is associated with antibodies against BP180 (Type XVII collagen), specifically the NC16A domain. DIF shows linear IgG and C3 at the BMZ. Tense bullae on erythematous base at flexural sites are typical.

questions.q: A 45-year-old patient on long-term dapsone for dermatitis herpetiformis develops sudden onset cyanosis, chocolate-brown blood, and dyspnea. What is the most likely complication?
questions.exp: Dapsone can cause methemoglobinemia, presenting with cyanosis and 'chocolate-brown' colored blood due to oxidation of hemoglobin iron from Fe2+ to Fe3+. Treatment is IV methylene blue. Hemolytic anemia is dose-dependent, while methemoglobinemia can occur with standard doses.

questions.q: A 30-year-old HIV-positive patient (CD4: 80 cells/μL) presents with extensive verrucous papules over the hands and perianal area. Biopsy shows koilocytes and large intranuclear viral inclusions. What HPV subtype is most likely responsible?
questions.exp: In epidermodysplasia verruciformis (EV) and immunocompromised patients (like HIV), HPV 5 and 8 are associated with diffuse verrucous lesions and high risk of malignant transformation. EV-related HPV types (5, 8, 9, 12, 14, 15, 17) are typically non-oncogenic in immunocompetent hosts.

questions.q: A 25-year-old presents with a sporotrichoid pattern of nodules along the lymphatics of the forearm following a thorn prick. KOH mount shows cigar-shaped yeast forms. What is the drug of choice?
questions.exp: Sporotrichosis caused by Sporothrix schenckii presents with a characteristic lymphocutaneous pattern. While SSKI (Potassium iodide) was the traditional treatment, Itraconazole 100–200 mg/day is the current drug of choice due to better efficacy and tolerability.

questions.q: A 50-year-old male presents with a pearly, translucent papule with telangiectasia and rolled borders on the nose. The lesion has been slowly enlarging for 2 years. What is the most common histological subtype?
questions.exp: Basal cell carcinoma (BCC) is the most common skin cancer. The nodular subtype is the most common, presenting as a pearly, shiny nodule with rolled edges, telangiectasia, and sometimes central ulceration ('rodent ulcer'). It occurs most commonly on sun-exposed areas of the face.

questions.q: A 68-year-old woman presents with an erythematous, well-defined plaque on the vulva with a 'strawberry' surface. Biopsy shows full-thickness epidermal atypia without dermal invasion. What is this lesion?
questions.exp: Erythroplasia of Queyrat is a form of carcinoma in situ (squamous cell carcinoma in situ) occurring on the glans penis or vulva, presenting as a bright red, velvety plaque. It shows full-thickness epidermal atypia on biopsy. It has a higher rate of progression to invasive SCC than Bowen's disease.

questions.q: A 35-year-old woman with SLE presents with discoid plaques, photosensitivity, and a butterfly rash. ANA is 1:640 (speckled pattern). Which antibody is most specific for SLE?
questions.exp: Anti-Sm (anti-Smith) antibody is the most specific antibody for SLE (specificity ~99%), though sensitivity is low (~25–30%). Anti-dsDNA is highly specific and correlates with disease activity and nephritis. Anti-Ro and anti-La are more associated with Sjögren's syndrome.

questions.q: A 45-year-old woman develops tight, hidebound skin over the fingers and face with difficulty opening the mouth. Pulmonary fibrosis is noted on HRCT. Which antibody is most strongly associated with pulmonary fibrosis in this condition?
questions.exp: In systemic sclerosis (SSc), anti-topoisomerase I (Scl-70) antibody is associated with diffuse cutaneous SSc and pulmonary fibrosis. Anti-centromere antibody is associated with limited cutaneous SSc (CREST syndrome) and pulmonary arterial hypertension. Anti-RNA pol III is associated with renal crisis.

questions.q: A 10-year-old child presents with intense pruritus and linear burrows in the finger webs. The child's 3 siblings are also affected. What is the best treatment for the entire household?
opts: 5% permethrin cream applied overnight, all members simultaneously
questions.exp: 5% permethrin cream is the drug of choice for scabies in children and adults. It should be applied to the entire body from neck down and left for 8–12 hours, with all household members treated simultaneously to prevent reinfestation. Lindane is neurotoxic and not preferred in children.

questions.q: A 60-year-old patient presents with Wickham's striae on the buccal mucosa and pruritic, violaceous, flat-topped papules on the flexor surfaces of the wrists. The pathological process is best described as:
opts: T-cell mediated cytotoxic attack on basal keratinocytes
IgA deposits in the papillary dermis
questions.exp: Lichen planus (LP) is a T-lymphocyte mediated autoimmune disorder where cytotoxic CD8+ T cells attack basal keratinocytes, leading to liquefaction degeneration (vacuolar change) of the basal layer. This results in apoptosis and formation of colloid (Civatte) bodies.

questions.q: A 20-year-old presents with diffuse non-scarring alopecia, positive hair pull test, and increased telogen count on trichogram. She had a febrile illness 3 months ago. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Telogen effluvium presents 2–4 months after a triggering event (fever, surgery, childbirth, severe stress) due to premature shift of anagen hairs to telogen. It results in diffuse non-scarring hair loss with positive hair pull test. Trichogram shows >25% telogen hairs.

questions.q: A patient is being treated with methotrexate for severe psoriasis. What is the most important baseline investigation to assess drug toxicity?
questions.exp: Before starting methotrexate, baseline LFTs, CBC, renal function, chest X-ray, and hepatitis B/C serology are essential. LFTs and CBC with differential are the most critical baseline investigations. PIIINP is a non-invasive marker for MTX-induced hepatic fibrosis used for monitoring.

questions.q: A 30-year-old male presents with well-defined erythematous plaques with silvery scales over the extensor surfaces of elbows and knees. Auspitz sign is positive. What is the characteristic histological finding?
opts: Munro's microabscesses and Kogoj's spongiform pustules
Colloid bodies and saw-tooth rete ridges
questions.exp: Psoriasis shows characteristic histology: parakeratosis, Munro's microabscesses (neutrophils in stratum corneum), Kogoj's spongiform pustules (neutrophils in spinous layer), acanthosis, elongated rete ridges with clubbing, and suprapapillary thinning of epidermis.

questions.q: A 55-year-old male with PUVA-treated psoriasis develops a persistent, keratotic, erythematous patch on the trunk. Biopsy shows atypical keratinocytes. This is best described as:
questions.exp: Long-term PUVA therapy increases the risk of squamous cell carcinoma and PUVA keratoses (dysplastic lesions resembling actinic keratoses). PUVA keratoses are irregular, keratotic, erythematous lesions with cytological atypia on biopsy, representing PUVA-induced carcinoma in situ.

questions.q: A 40-year-old woman presents with palpable purpura on the lower limbs with arthralgia, and hematuria. Biopsy shows leukocytoclastic vasculitis with IgA deposits on DIF. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Henoch-Schönlein Purpura (HSP), now called IgA vasculitis, is characterized by palpable purpura (usually lower limbs), arthritis, abdominal pain, and renal involvement (hematuria/proteinuria). DIF shows IgA deposits in small vessel walls. It is the most common systemic vasculitis in children but can occur in adults.

questions.q: A 25-year-old woman presents with recurrent blistering in areas of minor trauma, nail dystrophy, and milia formation. DIF shows IgG deposits at the BMZ below the lamina densa. What is the target antigen?
questions.exp: Epidermolysis bullosa acquisita (EBA) is an autoimmune bullous disorder with antibodies against Type VII collagen (anchoring fibrils). IIF on salt-split skin shows dermal (floor) staining. The classic form presents with mechanobullous features, milia, and nail dystrophy.

questions.q: A patient with long-standing leprosy develops sudden acute erythematous nodules over the face and extremities with fever, neutrophilia, and elevated ESR. Histology shows foam cells. What is this reaction?
questions.exp: Erythema nodosum leprosum (ENL) is a Type 2 lepra reaction occurring in lepromatous (LL) and borderline lepromatous (BL) patients. It is an immune complex-mediated (Type III) reaction presenting with tender erythematous nodules, fever, and systemic features. Histology shows foamy macrophages and neutrophilic infiltration.

questions.q: A 20-year-old male presents with grouped vesicles on an erythematous base over the lower lip. This is the third episode in 2 years. The most likely diagnosis and treatment are:
opts: Herpes zoster; valacyclovir 1g TID for 7 days
Herpes simplex labialis; acyclovir 400mg TID for 5 days or episodic therapy
questions.exp: Recurrent herpes labialis (HSL) is caused by HSV-1 reactivation. It presents with recurrent grouped vesicles on an erythematous base at the same site. Episodic therapy with acyclovir 400mg TID or 800mg BID for 5 days is effective. For frequent recurrences (>6/year), suppressive therapy (acyclovir 400mg BD) is recommended.

questions.q: A 48-year-old male presents with hyperpigmented, verrucous plaques on the extensor surfaces with 'cobblestone' appearance. He has had progressive difficulty climbing stairs. CK is elevated. The most likely skin manifestation is:
questions.exp: Gottron's papules are pathognomonic of dermatomyositis – flat-topped, violaceous or erythematous papules over the knuckles (MCP and PIP joints). Combined with proximal muscle weakness (difficulty climbing stairs) and elevated CK, this is dermatomyositis. The 'mechanics hands' and heliotrope rash are other features.

questions.q: A dermatologist performs a punch biopsy. The instrument used most commonly for punch biopsy in dermatology has a diameter of:
questions.exp: The standard punch biopsy instrument most commonly used in dermatology is 4 mm in diameter. It provides an adequate core for histopathological diagnosis. For small lesions, 3 mm punches may be used. Larger punches (6 mm or more) may be used for therapeutic excision of small lesions.

questions.q: A 55-year-old male presents with extensive tinea corporis not responding to topical antifungals for 6 weeks. KOH shows septate hyphae. The most appropriate next step is:
opts: Switch to a different topical antifungal
Oral fluconazole 150 mg weekly for 4 weeks
questions.exp: Extensive or recurrent tinea corporis not responding to topical antifungals warrants systemic therapy. Oral terbinafine 250 mg/day for 2–4 weeks is the most efficacious systemic antifungal for dermatophytosis due to its fungicidal action. It has better cure rates than itraconazole or griseofulvin for tinea infections.

questions.q: A 32-year-old female presents with symmetric hypopigmented macules over the dorsum of hands and face since 1 year. Wood's lamp examination shows chalk-white fluorescence. No sensation loss. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Vitiligo appears as chalk-white (blue-white) fluorescence under Wood's lamp examination, enhancing the depigmented areas. The macules are completely depigmented (not hypopigmented), symmetric, and have no sensation loss (differentiating from leprosy). Pityriasis versicolor shows yellow-green fluorescence.

questions.q: A 25-year-old male intravenous drug user presents with condyloma lata on the perianal area, lymphadenopathy, and maculopapular rash on the palms and soles. RPR is reactive 1:64. What stage of syphilis is this?
questions.exp: Secondary syphilis occurs 6–8 weeks after the primary chancre and presents with maculopapular rash (classically involving palms and soles), condyloma lata (moist, flat-topped papules in moist areas), lymphadenopathy, and mucous patches. RPR/VDRL are highly reactive in secondary syphilis.

questions.q: A 70-year-old male presents with an ulcerated growth on the lower lip with regional lymphadenopathy. Biopsy shows well-differentiated squamous cell carcinoma. The most important predisposing factor in this case is likely:
opts: Chronic sun exposure and pipe smoking
questions.exp: Squamous cell carcinoma of the lower lip is strongly associated with chronic sun exposure (actinic cheilitis) and tobacco/pipe smoking. The lower lip receives more UV radiation than the upper lip. HPV (types 16/18) is associated with SCC of the oral mucosa and anogenital region rather than the lip.

questions.q: A 16-year-old presents with comedones, inflammatory papules, and nodules over the face and trunk. He has previously failed topical retinoids and oral antibiotics. The most appropriate next line of treatment is:
questions.exp: Oral isotretinoin is the drug of choice for severe nodulo-cystic acne and acne unresponsive to conventional therapy. It targets all four pathogenic factors of acne (sebum production, follicular keratinization, P. acnes colonization, and inflammation). The standard dose is 0.5–1 mg/kg/day for 15–20 weeks (cumulative dose 120–150 mg/kg).
